rv.q: Neither prosaic nor clinical, it defies all expectations for a story in which the main character receives a fatal diagnosis, telling the tale in the most lively, surreal and surprising ways imaginable.
In its own roundabout way, this surreal new comedy might also be the most searingly astute drama of the Covid era.
I laughed pretty much nonstop, the exception being a few 'aww' moments which always stopped short of maudlin.

Though it goes overboard with obliqueness and presentational elements, it is ultimately an engaging effort, sustaining its 90-minute length due to its strong emotional core and the supreme Linda Lavin.
What leavens the often brutal approach to the young man's illness is that Lavin's character, while never ceasing to ask for and receive money, does develop empathy for him.
You Will Get Sick prompts more confusion than clarity, but a healthy helping of dry humor and a commitment to being daring and experimental for its own sake make it entertaining.
Linda Lavin, with her great comic timing, and Daniel K. Isaac, with his expressive skills clearly communicating confusion and suffering, make the most of their underwritten characters.
Over an interminable eighty-five minutes, playwright Noah Diaz's 'You Will Get Sick' meanders between absurdity and inanity, continually challenging the audience to distinguish one from the other.

Ms. Lavin...brings her earthy naturalism and comic timing to her every moment, her nasal inflections and subtextual cynicism giving the airy play the ballast of a palpable personality without which it might otherwise fly away.

cn.t: Diaz's absurdist meditation on mortality and caregiving divides critics: some praise its inventive staging and Lavin's performance, finding it charming and thought-provoking, while others dismiss it as indecipherable and meandering despite striking moments.
